title: 在 α=0.05 下运行 40 次检验，你的假阳性概率是 87%，不是 5%。我实测了
author: Devanshu Biswas
content:
Forty hypotheses, each tested at α = 0.05, nothing real going on. What is the chance you find at least one "significant" result?

87.2%. Measured across 20,000 simulated experiments. Theory says 1 − 0.95⁴⁰ = 87.1%.

All of it running in your browser: https://dev48.infy.uk/ml/day64-multiple-comparisons.html

First, check the null

Before any correction claim means anything, the null distribution has to actually be uniform, because every p-value method assumes it. So the page generates 20,000 p-values under a true null and bins them: worst decile 2.5% off flat.

Skip this and every number downstream is measuring your generator instead of your statistics.

Bonferroni, and why Holm strictly dominates it

Bonferroni: compare every p to α/m. Simple, correct, and needlessly harsh.

Holm sorts them and walks up, spending the budget as it goes: 

function holm(pvals, alpha){
  const idx = pvals.map((p, i) => [p, i]).sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0]);
  const m = pvals.length;
  const rejected = new Set();
  for (let k = 0; k < m; k++){
    const [p, i] = idx[k];
    if (p > alpha / (m - k)) break;        // step-DOWN: stop at the first failure
    rejected.add(i);
  }
  return rejected;
}

The first comparison is identical to Bonferroni; every later one is more generous. So Holm rejects a superset, at the same family-wise error control. That is provable, but the page measures it anyway: 11 wins, 1 tie, 0 losses across 12 configurations, and both stay at or under 5% FWER for m = 10, 40 and 120.

If you are using Bonferroni today, Holm is a strict upgrade for four lines of code.

FWER and FDR are different guarantees, not strong and weak versions of one

This is the part that gets taught badly.

  • FWER — the chance of any false positive. Bonferroni, Holm.
  • FDR — the expected fraction of your discoveries that are false. Benjamini-Hochberg.

Measured on the same data, m = 100 with 20 real effects:

procedure FDR FWER power
Holm ~0% ≤5% 32.0%
BH 4.11% 41.8% 60.5%

BH's family-wise error rate is 41.8% and that is not a bug. BH never promised to bound it. It promised that of the things it hands you, about 5% are wrong — and it kept that promise while finding nearly twice as many real effects.

Pick the guarantee that matches the decision. One irreversible expensive action on the winner: control FWER. A ranked list of 60 candidates for a follow-up screen: control FDR.

BH is step-UP, and getting that wrong is silent

The natural implementation walks up from the smallest p and stops at the first failure. That is BH's cousin, not BH. BH scans from the largest, finds the biggest k with p₍ₖ₎ ≤ kα/m, and rejects everything below it — including p-values that individually failed their own line: 

function benjaminiHochberg(pvals, alpha){
  const idx = pvals.map((p, i) => [p, i]).sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0]);
  const m = pvals.length;
  let kMax = -1;
  for (let k = 0; k < m; k++)
    if (idx[k][0] <= alpha * (k + 1) / m) kMax = k;   // LAST one that passes
  return new Set(idx.slice(0, kMax + 1).map(x => x[1]));
}

The two versions disagree on 102 of 3,000 experiments, and in 37 of 2,000 the correct one rejects a p-value above its own threshold. Both look fine on a spot check.

The trap in the results table

Bonferroni at m = 200 posts an FDR of 4.20% — apparently as good as BH.

It made 0.045 discoveries per experiment, and found 25.4% of real effects when 40 of the 200 were real.

A procedure that finds nothing has a wonderful false-discovery rate. Never read a rate column without the count column beside it.

The line worth remembering

Every correction is bought with power. Bonferroni buys the strongest guarantee at the highest price, Holm buys the same guarantee cheaper, BH buys a weaker guarantee much cheaper, BY buys BH's guarantee under arbitrary dependence for 25 points of power. There is no free option — only a choice about which error you can afford.

oneSentenceSummary: 在 α=0.05 下运行 40 次独立检验，至少出现一次假阳性的概率约为 87%；文章用代码和模拟解释了 Bonferroni、Holm 以及 FDR/FWER 之间的取舍。
summary: 文章从一个简单模拟开始：40 个原假设都以 α=0.05 检验，重复 20 000 次，结果显示至少得到一个“显著”结果的概率为 87.2%，与理论值 1−0.95⁴⁰ 吻合。随后文章讨论了多重检验校正。首先，它验证了任何 p 值方法都需要的均匀零分布。接着介绍了 Bonferroni 校正（α/m），并说明 Holm 的逐步递减法为何严格优于它——在相同家族错误率（FWER）控制下功效更高，并通过多种配置的经验验证。文章随后区分了 FWER 与 FDR，指出 Bonferroni 和 Holm 控制 FWER，而 Benjamini-Hochberg（BH）控制的是预期错误发现率。一张表格比较了在 100 个假设中有 20 个非原假设时 Holm 与 BH 在功效、FDR 和 FWER 上的表现，说明 BH 功效更高，但代价是更大的 FWER。文章进一步解释了 BH 的逐步递增实现，警告只看 FDR 率而不看发现数量会掉入陷阱，并总结道：每一次校正都是用功效换取错误控制，天下没有免费的午餐。全文提供了可运行的 JavaScript 代码，并附上交互演示链接，让概念更加具体。

mainPoints.point: 以 α=0.05 检验 40 个真实原假设，至少出现一次假阳性的概率约为 87%。
mainPoints.explanation: 模拟（20 000 次）和公式 1−0.95⁴⁰ 都证实了这种高假阳性风险，凸显了校正的必要性。

mainPoints.point: Holm 的逐步递减法严格优于 Bonferroni，同时保持 FWER ≤ α。
mainPoints.explanation: Holm 对 p 值排序并使用递减阈值；它会拒绝 Bonferroni 拒绝集合的超集，这一点已在多个 m 值下得到经验验证。

mainPoints.point: 当许多假设为非原假设时，BH 控制的是 FDR 而非 FWER，并可能带来显著更高的功效。
mainPoints.explanation: 在 100 个假设中有 20 个真实效应的情况下，BH 的功效约为 60.5%，FDR 为 4.11%；而 Holm 的功效只有约 32%，但 FWER 保持在 ≤5%。

keyQuotes: 每一次校正是用功效换来的。Bonferroni 以最高价格买下最强保证，Holm 用更便宜的价格买下同样的保证，BH 则用便宜得多的价格买下一个较弱的保证。
结果表中的陷阱：一个什么都没找到的程序，其错误发现率看起来会非常漂亮。因此绝不要只看比率列，而不看旁边的计数列。
